Mood: Solemn, tense and heavy with finality
Time of day: Late evening, dusk light fading to torchlight

Negatives: Avoid photorealism or a photographic look. Avoid childish/cartoonish styling. Palette: Mature, grounded color; rich but restrained contrast.
Lighting: Luminous, dramatic lighting.
Materials and texture: Gritty, raw texture; avoid polished digital smoothness.
Composition: Cinematic, immersive viewpoint; heroic but grounded.

1) No text or symbols anywhere: no letters, numbers, signage, logos or inscriptions, no writing on scrolls, tablets, books, boards or halos, and no artist's signature or initials in a corner.
2) One scene painted to every edge of the frame: no panels, collage, border, frame, margin, visible paper or blank backdrop, and never a photographed painting or mockup.
3) Nothing from outside the moment's era.
4) Natural anatomy: no extra or malformed limbs, hands or faces.
5) sexually explicit content and lingering gore are never shown; serious depictions of battles, blood, death and crucifixion and non-sexual nudity may be, treated seriously.
6) No likeness of any real actor, performer or public figure.
7) Show the SELECTED CHARACTERS with their canon. Anyone else appears only as an unnamed figure the scene plan describes.

SCENE: one moment of The Holy Bible, described by the scene plan below.

WORK BRIEF (bible-web; what may be shown; it outranks the style, the look and the plan):
Tone: Reverent, grounded and epic; grief, hope and human dignity without spectacle.

Depiction: Treat battles, death and crucifixion seriously; avoid lingering gore.
Depiction: No sexually explicit content; non-sexual nudity may follow the text.
Depiction: Show all peoples with dignity, without ethnic or religious caricature.
Depiction: Visionary creatures follow the text, strange and fearsome rather than comic.
Era: Egypt, wilderness and settlement
People: Israelites, Egyptians and neighboring ancient peoples.
Dress: Woven tunics, cloaks, Egyptian linen and priestly garments.
Buildings and objects: Tents, tabernacle, Egyptian palaces and fortified towns.
Technology: Bronze tools, chariots and early iron; no modern objects.

SELECTED CHARACTERS: Moses

UNSEEN PRESENCE (binding): the light, cloud, smoke, fire and wind in the scene plan are light and weather spread through the place, not one glowing shape. Nobody stands, sits or hovers in them.

CANON (fixed identity of the figures, places and things present; the scene plan decides pose, expression and action):
- Moses: an old man of about eighty; lean, weathered build; brown skin darkened by desert sun; white hair and a long white beard; deep-set, steady eyes and lined brow; a plain undyed linen tunic belted at the waist with a long dark-brown wool cloak; he carries a wooden shepherd's staff of dark acacia wood, and only he bears the rod of God.
- Red Sea: a wide, deep arm of open water between desert shores, its surface dark blue-green under wind. Sand dunes and low reddish cliffs line the coast; scattered tamarisk and palms grow at the water's edge. Bare rock outcrops and shallow wadis run down to the shore, and a distant fortified town sits on the northern ridge.

In his eyes she eclipses and predominates the whole of her sex. It was not that he felt any emotion akin to love for Irene Adler. All emotions, and that one particularly, were abhorrent to his cold, precise but admirably balanced mind. He was, I take it, the most perfect reasoning and observing machine that the world has seen, but as a lover he would have placed himself in a false position. Grit in a sensitive instrument, or a crack in one of his own high-power lenses, would not be more disturbing than a strong emotion in a nature such as his. In his eyes she eclipses and predominates the whole of her sex. It was not that he felt any emotion akin to love for Irene Adler. All emotions, and that one particularly, were abhorrent to his cold, precise but admirably balanced mind. He was, I take it, the most perfect reasoning and observing machine that the world has seen, but as a lover he would have placed himself in a false position. He never spoke of the softer passions, save with a gibe and a sneer. They were admirable things for the observer—excellent for drawing the veil from men’s motives and actions. But for the trained reasoner to admit such intrusions into his own delicate and finely adjusted temperament was to introduce a distracting factor which might throw a doubt upon all his mental results. Grit in a sensitive instrument, or a crack in one of his own high-power lenses, would not be more disturbing than a strong emotion in a nature such as his. And yet there was but one woman to him, and that woman was the late Irene Adler, of dubious and questionable memory."

If instructions conflict, follow these rules, then the work brief, then canon, then the art style, then the scene plan. SCENE: one moment of Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland, Who Stole the Tarts? ¶16 to Who Stole the Tarts? ¶28: "The first witness was the Hatter. He came in with a teacup in one hand and a piece of bread-and-butter in the other. “I beg pardon, your Majesty,” he began, “for bringing these in: but I hadn’t quite finished my tea when I was sent for.” “You ought to have finished,” said the King. “When did you begin?” The Hatter looked at the March Hare, who had followed him into the court, arm-in-arm with the Dormouse. “Fourteenth of March, I _think_ it was,” he said. “Fifteenth,” said the March Hare. “Sixteenth,” added the Dormouse. “Write that down,” the King said to the jury, and the jury eagerly wrote down all three dates on their slates, and then added them up, and reduced the answer to shillings and pence. “Take off your hat,” the King said to the Hatter. “It isn’t mine,” said the Hatter. “_Stolen!_” the King exclaimed, turning to the jury, who instantly made a memorandum of the fact. “I keep them to sell,” the Hatter added as an explanation; “I’ve none of my own. I’m a hatter.” Here the Queen put on her spectacles, and began staring at the Hatter, who turned pale and fidgeted. “Give your evidence,” said the King; “and don’t be nervous, or I’ll have you executed on the spot.” This did not…"

WORK BRIEF (alice-in-wonderland; what may be shown; it outranks the style, the look and the plan):
Tone: Whimsical and dreamlike, with a gently unsettling bewilderment that turns to sharp absurdity at court.
Depiction: Alice's changing size reads clearly against doors, furniture, trees and other figures.
Depiction: Talking animals are drawn as animals, with human posture and dress where the text gives it.
Depiction: Playing-card courtiers, gardeners and soldiers are flat, oblong cards with heads, arms and legs.
Depiction: Threats and executions stay threats or slapstick; no gore or real injury.
Depiction: Take no likeness, costume or prop from film or animated adaptations.
Era: Victorian England and its dream Wonderland
People: Alice, a young Victorian English girl, among talking animals, card courtiers and odd Wonderland folk.
Dress: A Victorian child's dress and pinafore for Alice; period robes, waistcoats and hats for others.
Buildings and objects: Riverbank, rabbit-hole, long hall, little door, cottages, mushroom wood, croquet-ground and courtroom.
Technology: Pocket watches, oil lamps, slates and pencils; no machines or modern devices.

SELECTED CHARACTERS: Hatter; King of Hearts; Queen of Hearts; the jury; March Hare; the Dormouse

CANON (fixed identity of the figures, places and things present; the scene plan decides pose, expression and action):
- Hatter: an adult Victorian man of middle years, lean and slightly stooped, with untidy hair in need of cutting and a long pale face. He wears a shabby period waistcoat and frock coat with a tall, battered hat that is sometimes not his own. Colours are faded browns and greys with a dingy cravat. He carries a teacup and a slice of bread-and-butter, and an old pocket watch.
- King of Hearts: an elderly, mild, timid man of about sixty with a short grey-white beard and mild anxious face, wearing a tall gold crown set over a great white judge's wig, round spectacles, and a long crimson royal robe with ermine trim over a white waistcoat and knee breeches. Flat oblong playing-card body with head, arms and legs at the corners, decorated with red hearts. Carries a small sceptre in one gloved hand.
- Queen of Hearts: a flat, oblong playing-card royal with a head, arms and legs, drawn as an imperious adult woman of middle age with a stern, frowning face and a commanding bearing. Her hair is dark and bound under a small golden crown. Her skin is fair. Her signature outfit is a long crimson velvet gown with a wide golden-edged collar, trimmed with heart motifs, in deep red and gold. Her signature prop is a rounded golden sceptre held in one hand.
- the jury: twelve creatures, a mix of animals and birds, each drawn as an animal or bird with human posture and period dress such as waistcoats and hats; they sit in the jury-box, each holding a slate and pencil. Their forms vary, including a lizard among them. Flat card-like jury members are not used; they are animal and bird figures.
- March Hare: an anthropomorphic hare standing upright with human posture and dress, long upright ears, brown-and-tawny fur, adult in age, lean and slightly hunched build, a long muzzle with whiskers, round wide-set eyes, a wild restless look. He wears a rumpled period waistcoat, shirt and tailcoat in muted brown and cream, with a loose cravat and a tall hat tilted askew. He carries a teacup or teapot as his signature prop.
- the Dormouse: a small, drowsy talking dormouse, grey-brown fur with a pale belly, round ears, a thin tail and small whiskers, standing and sitting upright in human posture. Age: adult. Build: slight and plump. Skin: grey-brown fur. Face: small dark eyes that are often shut, a pink nose, long whiskers. Signature outfit: a faded blue waistcoat with a small brass button and a dull green neckcloth. Signature prop: a china teacup held in its small paws.
- The Queen of Hearts' court of justice: a large, crowded courtroom of tall, sombre stone walls and a high roof, with a raised royal throne for the King and Queen of Hearts at one end, a judge's great wig-marked bench, and a jury-box holding twelve jurors writing on slates. In the centre stands a long table bearing a large dish of tarts, and the floor is strewn with a crowd of little birds, beasts and flat playing-card courtiers. Doors lead off to the side, scattered papers litter the floor, and the space is formal and dim.
- Only Hatter, King of Hearts, Queen of Hearts, the jury, March Hare, the Dormouse, The Queen of Hearts' court of justice have this canon look; other selected people get clearly different faces, hair and clothing colours.

SCENE PLAN (this moment's place, time and action; obey the rules, brief, canon and style):
Primary subject: The nervous Hatter, a thin man in a rumpled hat-maker's coat, teacup in one hand and bread-and-butter in the other, mid-shift from foot to foot.
Action: He bites a large piece out of his teacup instead of the bread-and-butter while glancing uneasily at the Queen.
Setting: A crowded Wonderland courtroom with a raised bench for the King and Queen, card-shaped courtiers lining the walls, and a jury box.
Secondary elements: The jury leaning forward with slates on their knees, the March Hare and Dormouse beside the Hatter, the King seated and watching, the Queen peering through her spectacles, and card officers standing at attention.
Mood: Tense, comically anxious and absurd, with the witness rattled by the court's menace.
Time of day: Indoors under even lamplight, with no sky visible.
Composition: Wide view of the courtroom from the floor, with the Hatter centred in the foreground and the King and Queen framed high on the bench behind him.

ART STYLE: Ink & Watercolor
Rendering: Pen-and-ink drawing with transparent watercolor washes laid over the whole picture; a finished watercolor painting of the work's world, not a sketch.
Negatives: Washes, pigment and scenery must reach every edge. No white or cream paper margins, unpainted corners, paper edges, sketchbook, tape, border or vignette. Do not present the scene on a sheet of paper or against a blank backdrop. Avoid photorealism, digital airbrush smoothness and cartoon caricature.
Palette: Transparent washes of ochre, sienna, indigo and sage covering the whole picture, sky and corners included.
Lighting: Clear natural light; shadows as cool layered washes.
Materials and texture: Confident ink linework, wet-in-wet blooms and granulating pigment within the depicted world.
Composition: A complete scene: setting, sky and ground painted out to every edge and corner, with detail concentrated on key subjects.

NARRATIVE CONTINUITY (cues only; compose the current moment):
- After: Just at this moment Alice felt a very curious sensation, which puzzled her a good deal until she made out what it was: she was beginning to grow larger again, and she thought at first she would get up and leave the cour…

SCENE PRESENTATION:
- Depict the moment directly, as if the viewer is present inside the scene.
- Extend scenery, sky, darkness, architecture or atmosphere all the way to the edges and corners.
Aspect ratio: 16:9 (WIDESCREEN landscape).

messages.content:
PRIORITY RULES:
1) No text or symbols anywhere: no letters, numbers, signage, logos or inscriptions, no writing on labels, bottles, books, signs, slates or playing cards, and no artist's signature or initials in a corner.
2) One scene painted to every edge of the frame: no panels, collage, border, frame, margin, visible paper or blank backdrop, and never a photographed painting or mockup.
3) Nothing from outside the moment's era.
4) Natural anatomy: no extra or malformed limbs, hands or faces.
5) sexually explicit content and lingering gore are never shown; serious depictions of battles, blood and death and non-sexual nudity may be, treated seriously.
6) No likeness of any real actor, performer or public figure.
7) Show the SELECTED CHARACTERS with their canon. Anyone else appears only as an unnamed figure the scene plan describes.
If instructions conflict, follow these rules, then the work brief, then canon, then the art style, then the scene plan. The text decides who is in the scene; canon decides how they look; the scene plan decides this moment's place, time, light, clothing and action. Owner look constraints, when given, are binding.

SCENE: one moment of Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland, Who Stole the Tarts? ¶16 to Who Stole the Tarts? ¶28: "The first witness was the Hatter. He came in with a teacup in one hand and a piece of bread-and-butter in the other. “I beg pardon, your Majesty,” he began, “for bringing these in: but I hadn’t quite finished my tea when I was sent for.” “You ought to have finished,” said the King. “When did you begin?” The Hatter looked at the March Hare, who had followed him into the court, arm-in-arm with the Dormouse. “Fourteenth of March, I _think_ it was,” he said. “Fifteenth,” said the March Hare. “Sixteenth,” added the Dormouse. “Write that down,” the King said to the jury, and the jury eagerly wrote down all three dates on their slates, and then added them up, and reduced the answer to shillings and pence. “Take off your hat,” the King said to the Hatter. “It isn’t mine,” said the Hatter. “_Stolen!_” the King exclaimed, turning to the jury, who instantly made a memorandum of the fact. “I keep them to sell,” the Hatter added as an explanation; “I’ve none of my own. I’m a hatter.” Here the Queen put on her spectacles, and began staring at the Hatter, who turned pale and fidgeted. “Give your evidence,” said the King; “and don’t be nervous, or I’ll have you executed on the spot.” This did not…"

WORK BRIEF (alice-in-wonderland; what may be shown; it outranks the style, the look and the plan):
Tone: Whimsical and dreamlike, with a gently unsettling bewilderment that turns to sharp absurdity at court.
Depiction: Alice's changing size reads clearly against doors, furniture, trees and other figures.
Depiction: Talking animals are drawn as animals, with human posture and dress where the text gives it.
Depiction: Playing-card courtiers, gardeners and soldiers are flat, oblong cards with heads, arms and legs.
Depiction: Threats and executions stay threats or slapstick; no gore or real injury.
Depiction: Take no likeness, costume or prop from film or animated adaptations.
Era: Victorian England and its dream Wonderland
People: Alice, a young Victorian English girl, among talking animals, card courtiers and odd Wonderland folk.
Dress: A Victorian child's dress and pinafore for Alice; period robes, waistcoats and hats for others.
Buildings and objects: Riverbank, rabbit-hole, long hall, little door, cottages, mushroom wood, croquet-ground and courtroom.
Technology: Pocket watches, oil lamps, slates and pencils; no machines or modern devices.

SELECTED CHARACTERS: Hatter; King of Hearts; Queen of Hearts; the jury; March Hare; the Dormouse

CANON (fixed identity of the figures, places and things present; the scene plan decides pose, expression and action):
- Hatter: an adult Victorian man of middle years, lean and slightly stooped, with untidy hair in need of cutting and a long pale face. He wears a shabby period waistcoat and frock coat with a tall, battered hat that is sometimes not his own. Colours are faded browns and greys with a dingy cravat. He carries a teacup and a slice of bread-and-butter, and an old pocket watch.
- King of Hearts: an elderly, mild, timid man of about sixty with a short grey-white beard and mild anxious face, wearing a tall gold crown set over a great white judge's wig, round spectacles, and a long crimson royal robe with ermine trim over a white waistcoat and knee breeches. Flat oblong playing-card body with head, arms and legs at the corners, decorated with red hearts. Carries a small sceptre in one gloved hand.
- Queen of Hearts: a flat, oblong playing-card royal with a head, arms and legs, drawn as an imperious adult woman of middle age with a stern, frowning face and a commanding bearing. Her hair is dark and bound under a small golden crown. Her skin is fair. Her signature outfit is a long crimson velvet gown with a wide golden-edged collar, trimmed with heart motifs, in deep red and gold. Her signature prop is a rounded golden sceptre held in one hand.
- the jury: twelve creatures, a mix of animals and birds, each drawn as an animal or bird with human posture and period dress such as waistcoats and hats; they sit in the jury-box, each holding a slate and pencil. Their forms vary, including a lizard among them. Flat card-like jury members are not used; they are animal and bird figures.
- March Hare: an anthropomorphic hare standing upright with human posture and dress, long upright ears, brown-and-tawny fur, adult in age, lean and slightly hunched build, a long muzzle with whiskers, round wide-set eyes, a wild restless look. He wears a rumpled period waistcoat, shirt and tailcoat in muted brown and cream, with a loose cravat and a tall hat tilted askew. He carries a teacup or teapot as his signature prop.
- the Dormouse: a small, drowsy talking dormouse, grey-brown fur with a pale belly, round ears, a thin tail and small whiskers, standing and sitting upright in human posture. Age: adult. Build: slight and plump. Skin: grey-brown fur. Face: small dark eyes that are often shut, a pink nose, long whiskers. Signature outfit: a faded blue waistcoat with a small brass button and a dull green neckcloth. Signature prop: a china teacup held in its small paws.
- The Queen of Hearts' court of justice: a large, crowded courtroom of tall, sombre stone walls and a high roof, with a raised royal throne for the King and Queen of Hearts at one end, a judge's great wig-marked bench, and a jury-box holding twelve jurors writing on slates. In the centre stands a long table bearing a large dish of tarts, and the floor is strewn with a crowd of little birds, beasts and flat playing-card courtiers. Doors lead off to the side, scattered papers litter the floor, and the space is formal and dim.
- Only Hatter, King of Hearts, Queen of Hearts, the jury, March Hare, the Dormouse, The Queen of Hearts' court of justice have this canon look; other selected people get clearly different faces, hair and clothing colours.

SCENE PLAN (this moment's place, time and action; obey the rules, brief, canon and style):
Primary subject: The nervous Hatter, a thin man in a rumpled hat-maker's coat, teacup in one hand and bread-and-butter in the other, mid-shift from foot to foot.
Action: He bites a large piece out of his teacup instead of the bread-and-butter while glancing uneasily at the Queen.
Setting: A crowded Wonderland courtroom with a raised bench for the King and Queen, card-shaped courtiers lining the walls, and a jury box.
Secondary elements: The jury leaning forward with slates on their knees, the March Hare and Dormouse beside the Hatter, the King seated and watching, the Queen peering through her spectacles, and card officers standing at attention.
Mood: Tense, comically anxious and absurd, with the witness rattled by the court's menace.
Time of day: Indoors under even lamplight, with no sky visible.
Composition: Wide view of the courtroom from the floor, with the Hatter centred in the foreground and the King and Queen framed high on the bench behind him.

ART STYLE: Classical
Rendering: Stylized, painterly, mysterious and expansive. The painterly treatment belongs to the depicted world itself, not to a photographed physical artwork.
Negatives: Avoid photorealism or a photographic look. Avoid childish/cartoonish styling. Never present the scene as a painting on a wall, gallery piece, framed artwork, fresco, mural, poster, manuscript page, or printed illustration. Do not show canvas texture, paper edges, matting, border, mockup, or surrounding room. The depicted world must fill the image edge-to-edge.
Palette: Mature, grounded color; rich but restrained contrast.
Lighting: Luminous, dramatic lighting.
Materials and texture: Gritty, raw texture; avoid polished digital smoothness.
Composition: Cinematic, immersive viewpoint; heroic but grounded.

NARRATIVE CONTINUITY (cues only; compose the current moment):
- After: Just at this moment Alice felt a very curious sensation, which puzzled her a good deal until she made out what it was: she was beginning to grow larger again, and she thought at first she would get up and leave the cour…

SCENE PRESENTATION:
- Depict the moment directly, as if the viewer is present inside the scene.
- Extend scenery, sky, darkness, architecture or atmosphere all the way to the edges and corners.
Aspect ratio: 16:9 (WIDESCREEN landscape).
